paragraphs: Anticipatory movement control must account for delays and for body systems that respond at different speeds. This paper develops counterfactual predictive control, an architecture inspired by the interaction between reactive motor feedback and the cerebellum’s adaptive anticipatory contribution. Its feed-forward module guides a feedback controller by supplying signals that provoke corrective reactions.

These signals are counterfactual: they act like error signals without representing actual present or future errors. To determine how the anticipatory module should learn, the authors derive a synaptic learning rule involving an eligibility trace. The trace combines a history of earlier synaptic inputs with error signals, extending beyond learning based only on events occurring together.

Applied to cerebellar physiology, the derivation implies that Purkinje cell synapses should construct these traces using a forward model of the controlled system. This is a consequence of the proposed control framework. For engineering, the contribution is an anticipatory architecture whose learning rule incorporates the dynamics of the complete feedback loop, connecting the timing of past inputs to their later control effects.
neurips-2016-a-forward-model-at-purkinje.tldr: A cerebellum-inspired control architecture derives a synaptic learning rule that uses system dynamics to support anticipatory movement.

paragraphs: Learning visual similarity without labels is difficult when each example supplies only one positive training instance against many negatives. Relationships between examples can also be unreliable, making it hard to train a convolutional network consistently. CliqueCNN addresses this problem by organizing the relationships used for training before asking the network to learn a shared representation.

Starting from weak estimates of local distance, the method solves an optimization problem that constructs batches with mutually consistent relationships. Similar examples form compact groups called cliques, while conflicting relationships are placed in different batches. Training then becomes a sequence of tasks in which the network categorizes examples by their clique membership.

Through these tasks, the network consolidates transitive relationships within and between cliques into one representation covering all samples. The method requires no labels, although it does begin with weak local similarity information. The reported results are competitive on detailed posture analysis and object classification. These findings support the usefulness of arranging imperfect similarity evidence into coherent training tasks for unsupervised visual learning.
neurips-2016-cliquecnn-deep-unsupervised.tldr: CliqueCNN learns visual representations without labels by grouping similar examples into cliques and separating conflicting relationships across training batches.

paragraphs: Influence maximization asks which initial nodes should be selected to encourage contagion through a network. Exact influence computation is generally NP-hard, so evaluating candidate selections can itself be a major obstacle. This paper develops efficiently computable upper and lower bounds on the influence of a selected set of nodes.

One family of bounds targets linear threshold models. Another applies to the broader class of triggering models, which includes independent cascade models. The authors quantify the separation between their upper and lower bounds for the linear threshold case and illustrate improvements in upper bounds for independent cascade models relative to existing results.

A key property is that the lower bounds are monotonic and submodular: adding nodes cannot decrease the bound, and additional nodes offer diminishing returns. This structure supports a greedy optimization guarantee with a factor of 1 − 1/e for the lower-bound objective. Combined with the influence bounds, it provides a scalable approach with rigorous guarantees, allowing optimization to proceed without repeatedly computing exact influence.
neurips-2016-computing-and-maximizing-in.tldr: Efficient influence bounds support scalable greedy optimization across several contagion models, with guarantees grounded in submodular lower bounds.

paragraphs: Data programming addresses the expense of manually labeling large training sets. Users write labeling functions: programs that assign heuristic labels to portions of the data. These programs can be inaccurate and disagree with one another, so their outputs need a way to account for noise before they become useful supervision.

The paper treats the labeling functions as implicitly specifying a generative model of labeling noise. It shows how recovering that model’s parameters can help denoise the resulting training set, with theoretical recovery guarantees established in several settings. It also modifies discriminative training losses to account for noise and demonstrates the approach with models including logistic regression and LSTMs.

On the 2014 TAC-KBP Slot Filling challenge, the authors report a result that would have won the competition. Applying data programming to an LSTM also improves its score by almost six F1 points over a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline. Initial user studies suggest that programming labeling rules may make model creation easier for non-experts when labeled data is scarce or absent.
neurips-2016-data-programming-creating-l.tldr: Data programming turns noisy labeling programs into training supervision by modeling their errors and adapting downstream learning to label uncertainty.

paragraphs: Neural translation depends heavily on paired sentences in two languages, which are costly to label. This paper develops dual-NMT to learn from monolingual text by connecting translation in opposite directions. An English-to-French model and a French-to-English model form a loop, creating feedback that can train both systems without a human labeling each new example.

The two models act as agents that teach one another through reinforcement learning. Feedback includes how plausible a translation looks to a language model and how well translating it back reconstructs the original sentence. Policy-gradient methods can use these signals to update the models iteratively, making the reverse translation task part of the learning process.

Experiments report strong results for translation between English and French. Specifically, for French-to-English translation, learning from monolingual data after a warm start using 10% of the bilingual data achieves accuracy comparable to training NMT on the full bilingual set. That result supports reducing paired-data requirements in the tested setting while retaining a bilingual initialization.
neurips-2016-dual-learning-for-machine-t.tldr: Dual-NMT trains opposite translation directions together, using monolingual text and round-trip feedback to reduce reliance on bilingual training pairs.

paragraphs: Many applications represent data with low-rank matrices, including recommendation, topic modeling, and source separation. When the underlying relationships change over time, a static matrix can miss useful temporal structure. This paper investigates how to recover an evolving low-rank matrix from incomplete observations and supplies theory for the potential benefits of using its dynamics.

The authors propose locally weighted matrix smoothing, or LOWEMS, as a framework for dynamic recovery under an exact low-rank constraint. They establish recovery error bounds for two observation settings: matrix sensing and matrix completion. Studying both settings broadens the analysis beyond a single way of observing only part of a matrix.

The bounds quantify how exploiting dynamic constraints can improve recovery accuracy and reduce sample requirements. This provides theoretical support for temporal modeling, whose practical advantages had received more attention than its guarantees. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate the potential benefits. The contribution is thus both a recovery framework and an analysis of when temporal information can be valuable.
neurips-2016-dynamic-matrix-recovery-fro.tldr: LOWEMS recovers evolving low-rank matrices from incomplete observations, with error bounds quantifying potential gains from temporal structure.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed losses allow unusually large errors, making learning-rate analysis harder than when losses are bounded. This paper studies conditions under which learning can still improve faster than the familiar rate proportional to one over the square root of the sample size. Its results accommodate losses that need not be bounded.

The analysis introduces two requirements. First, an envelope covering the absolute losses across the hypothesis class must exist and have a finite r-th moment. Second, the loss must satisfy a multi-scale Bernstein condition on that class. Together, these assumptions provide the control needed to establish faster rates despite the possibility of large loss values.

Under these conditions, the authors prove rates faster than O(n⁻¹ᐟ²). Depending on the moment parameter and the powers in the Bernstein condition, the rates can approach O(n⁻¹) arbitrarily closely. They also verify the assumptions for vector quantization using k-means with heavy-tailed distributions. This application shows how the general conditions yield concrete guarantees beyond bounded-loss settings.
neurips-2016-fast-learning-rates-with-he.tldr: Fast learning rates remain possible with heavy-tailed losses under moment and multi-scale Bernstein conditions, including for k-means vector quantization.

paragraphs: Standard generative clustering models often imply that cluster sizes grow proportionally with the dataset. This can be a poor match for entity resolution, where records are grouped according to the real entity they refer to. Adding many records about other entities should not require an existing entity’s group to occupy a fixed share of the enlarged dataset.

The paper formalizes an alternative called the microclustering property. It requires cluster sizes to grow sublinearly with the total number of observations, so each cluster becomes a negligible fraction of the dataset. This requirement permits growth while capturing the small-group behavior needed in the motivating applications.

The authors introduce a class of models capable of exhibiting microclustering and compare models from this class with two commonly used clustering models on four entity-resolution datasets. The central contribution is to make cluster-size scaling an explicit modeling choice. It supplies a framework for applications where conventional assumptions about how groups expand with the dataset are inappropriate.
neurips-2016-flexible-models-for-microcl.tldr: Microclustering models allow clusters to remain a vanishing fraction of growing datasets, matching the needs of applications such as entity resolution.

paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box function can be expensive when each evaluation requires a costly experiment or real-world interaction. Cheaper approximations, such as simulations, may provide useful guidance. This paper studies how to use several levels of evaluation fidelity so that inexpensive information helps concentrate costly measurements in promising regions.

The authors formulate a multi-fidelity bandit problem in which the target function and its approximations are sampled from a Gaussian process. Their method, MF-GP-UCB, uses upper confidence bounds to guide optimization. The intended behavior is to rule out low-value regions with cheap evaluations and reserve evaluations of the target function for a smaller, more promising region.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method exhibits this behavior and achieves better regret than strategies that ignore multi-fidelity information within the analyzed setting. Experiments on synthetic and real problems also report improvements over those strategies and other multi-fidelity approaches. The findings connect a practical allocation of evaluation costs with formal optimization guarantees.
neurips-2016-gaussian-process-bandit-opt.tldr: MF-GP-UCB uses cheap approximations to narrow the search before spending expensive evaluations on promising regions.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction for classification should preserve information that separates classes. This paper approaches that goal through a connection between multiclass boosting and support vector machines. Both combine a mapping of the data with linear classifiers and seek a large multiclass margin, but they assign learning to different parts of that construction.

In the described SVM formulation, the kernel determines the mapping while the linear classifiers are optimized. In boosting, the linear classifiers are fixed and a combination of weak learners builds the mapping. The authors argue that this intermediate prediction representation retains discriminative information, suggesting that controlling its dimension can produce useful compact embeddings.

Their method, Large Margin Discriminant Dimensionality Reduction, or LADDER, jointly learns the mapping and the linear classifiers efficiently. It produces a data-driven representation with a chosen number of dimensions. Experiments show that the resulting embeddings can significantly improve hashing and image or scene classification. The contribution ties representation size directly to a supervised separation objective.
neurips-2016-large-margin-discriminant-d.tldr: LADDER jointly learns a compact data representation and linear classifiers using a shared large-margin view of boosting and SVMs.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution depends on prior knowledge about plausible high-resolution image structure. Existing approaches learn this knowledge from paired low- and high-resolution patches or estimate it from the input image itself. The paper identifies difficulties with both: paired-patch methods can struggle with blurred inputs, while input-based estimation is affected by frequency aliasing.

The proposed approach combines these two information sources. It learns parametric sparse priors for the desired high-resolution patches using both the observed low-resolution image and a training image dataset. This lets the prior draw on the particular input while also incorporating information from external training images.

With those priors learned, the method solves a sparse coding problem to recover sparse codes and the corresponding high-resolution patches. Experiments report improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in both subjective appearance and objective image quality. The findings support the paper’s central design choice: combining input-specific evidence and dataset knowledge when estimating the image prior used for reconstruction.
neurips-2016-learning-parametric-sparse-.tldr: The method improves image super-resolution by learning sparse priors jointly from the input image and an external training dataset.

paragraphs: This paper studies binary classification when labels are randomly flipped with probability 1 − α. The parameter α measures the degree of supervision. The central question is how changing label reliability affects both the best possible statistical accuracy and the computational effort needed to reach that accuracy.

The authors establish two boundaries: the minimax accuracy achievable by algorithms without computational restrictions, and the accuracy achievable by polynomial-time algorithms under an oracle computational model. Comparing these boundaries separates what the data makes statistically possible from what computationally efficient procedures can attain within that model.

For small α, the analysis finds a gap between the boundaries, representing a computational price associated with weak supervision. The gap narrows as α increases. Thus, in the studied setting, more correct labels improve the optimal statistical accuracy and make that accuracy more accessible computationally. The result gives a theoretical account of why additional supervision can provide benefits beyond simply reducing label noise.
neurips-2016-more-supervision-less-compu.tldr: Under an oracle computational model, stronger supervision narrows the gap between statistically optimal classification and what polynomial-time algorithms can achieve.

paragraphs: Statistical physics had supplied a conjectured formula for mutual information in certain Bayesian matrix estimation problems, but rigorous proofs covered only limited cases. This paper proves the formula for symmetric rank-one matrix estimation in the Bayes-optimal setting. The result turns a heuristic prediction into a mathematical foundation for analyzing this class of problems.

The formula allows the authors to express the smallest achievable mean-square estimation error and characterize detectability transitions across problems including community detection and sparse principal component analysis. They also show that approximate message passing reaches Bayes-optimal performance for a large set of parameters. A gap nevertheless remains between currently known polynomial-time algorithms and information-theoretic expectations.

The proof combines interpolation methods from statistical physics, analysis of approximate message passing, and spatial coupling with threshold saturation from coding theory. This combination is itself a contribution: the authors describe the approach as generic and applicable to other statistical estimation problems with available physics-based predictions. Its immediate achievement remains the rigorous symmetric rank-one result.
neurips-2016-mutual-information-for-symm.tldr: A rigorous replica-formula proof characterizes information and estimation limits for symmetric rank-one matrices and establishes broad regimes of message-passing optimality.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement-learning tasks consist of repeated, finite interactions, such as a dialogue or a sequence of advertisement decisions. Their transition dynamics may depend on the stage of the interaction. This paper develops a probably approximately correct algorithm for finite episodic Markov decision processes that allows this time dependence.

Its guarantee bounds the number of episodes in which behavior is more than ε away from optimal. With confidence controlled by δ, that number is O(SAH³/ε² log(1/δ)), where S counts states, A counts actions, and H is the episode horizon. The algorithm has polynomial computational complexity, and the analysis accommodates approximate solutions to its internal planning problems.

The bound depends linearly on both the number of states and the number of actions, improving earlier quadratic state dependence in this setting. It also has lower horizon dependence than the cited infinite-horizon methods with linear state dependence. The resulting sample complexity is optimal up to a factor of H, identifying the remaining gap in the guarantee.
neurips-2016-only-h-is-left-near-tight-e.tldr: A polynomial-time episodic reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves a PAC sample bound linear in states and actions and optimal up to one horizon factor.

paragraphs: Sensor observations do not always arrive at regular intervals. Event-driven sensors can emit sparse, asynchronous signals, and different sensors may update at different rates. Phased LSTM adapts recurrent sequence modeling to this setting by making the timing of memory updates an explicit part of the network architecture.

The model extends an LSTM unit with a time gate controlled by a parameterized oscillation. Its memory cell updates during only a small portion of each cycle. This creates sparse updates while allowing the network to integrate inputs with arbitrary sampling rates and process asynchronous events whose timing carries useful information.

Despite updating memory less often, the paper reports faster convergence than regular LSTMs on tasks requiring learning over long sequences. It also reports improved performance in standard recurrent-network applications with an order of magnitude fewer computations. These findings suggest that selective updates can help both computational efficiency and sequence learning, while the time gate supplies a natural mechanism for handling irregularly timed observations.
neurips-2016-phased-lstm-accelerating-re.tldr: Phased LSTM adds an oscillating time gate that enables sparse memory updates, faster reported convergence, and natural handling of asynchronous inputs.

paragraphs: Differential privacy composition tracks the privacy cost of running several analyses on data. This paper considers a more adaptive setting: both the number of analyses and their privacy parameters can depend on earlier outputs. That flexibility goes beyond choosing algorithms adaptively while fixing all privacy parameters in advance.

The authors define two tools for different needs. A privacy filter stops a computation before it exceeds a predetermined privacy budget. A privacy odometer tracks privacy loss along the way without requiring such a budget beforehand. Separating these roles makes it possible to formulate guarantees when the analyst’s parameter choices evolve during the computation.

The paper shows that filters can achieve bounds comparable, up to constants, to existing composition theorems. Its odometer nearly matches non-adaptive composition bounds but sometimes incurs an additional small asymptotic factor. A lower-bound result shows that this overhead is unavoidable for valid adaptive odometers. Thus, enforcing a budget and accounting for privacy as one goes have provably different costs in this setting.
neurips-2016-privacy-odometers-and-filte.tldr: When privacy parameters are chosen adaptively, stopping at a fixed budget and tracking privacy loss without one have provably different accounting costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a real or complex vector from measurements that give squared magnitudes of inner products. These quadratic equations discard information about a global sign or phase, and solving such systems is NP-hard in general. The proposed algorithm, truncated generalized gradient flow, targets recovery in the random-system setting.

The algorithm has two stages. An orthogonality-promoting initialization uses simple power iterations to produce a starting estimate. Subsequent truncated generalized-gradient updates refine it using an amplitude-based objective that is both nonconvex and nonsmooth. The initialization and refinement are designed to work together while keeping the computation scalable.

The authors prove high-probability exact recovery, up to a global unit-magnitude factor, once the number of equations is on the order of the number of unknowns. The stated computational complexity scales linearly with the time needed to read the data. Numerical tests report more accurate and robust initialization than spectral alternatives and better refinement than Wirtinger-based methods even when initialization is held fixed.
neurips-2016-solving-random-systems-of-q.tldr: TGGF combines orthogonality-promoting initialization with truncated gradient refinement to recover vectors efficiently from random quadratic measurements.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks a vector with few nonzero entries from fewer observations than unknowns. Recovering its support means identifying which entries are nonzero. This paper studies support recovery with an ℓ₁ regularizer and nonsmooth data-fitting losses, concentrating on ℓ₁ and ℓ∞ losses and contrasting them with the usual ℓ₂ case.

The authors extend support-stability theory to these nonsmooth losses, which are used for sparse or uniform noise models. They derive a sharp condition ensuring that small additive observation noise leaves the recovered support stable, provided the loss constraint is scaled proportionally to the noise level. This explicitly connects the guarantee to both the problem structure and the tuning choice.

The theory also describes cases where the original support is unstable. It identifies an extended support that remains stable under small additive noise, giving structure to the failure of exact support stability. Numerical compressed-sensing analyses illustrate regimes ranging from complete stability to progressively greater instability, showing how the choice of loss affects which support behavior arises.
neurips-2016-sparse-support-recovery-wit.tldr: The paper establishes support-stability conditions for sparse recovery with nonsmooth losses and identifies stable extended supports when exact support stability fails.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems combine a data-fitting term with two separate regularizers. Treating the entire objective as one unit may overlook computational advantages available for its individual pieces. This paper proposes a stochastic method for minimizing a sum of three convex functions, handling one through stochastic gradients and the other two through their own proximal operators.

The smooth function is assumed to have a Lipschitz-continuous gradient and restricted strong convexity. The method is especially suitable when estimating that term’s gradient and processing the remaining terms separately is computationally advantageous. Doubly regularized empirical risk minimization is one motivating setting for this decomposition.

The algorithm works in the primal space and extends three-operator splitting to stochastic optimization. The authors establish convergence in expectation under standard assumptions on the stochastic gradient estimate. Numerical evidence on real-world problems supports its effectiveness. The contribution is a way to retain the useful three-part structure of an objective while allowing noisy, potentially cheaper gradient information for its smooth component.
neurips-2016-stochastic-three-composite-.tldr: A stochastic three-operator method optimizes convex objectives using a gradient estimate for one term and separate proximal updates for two others.

paragraphs: Sample compression studies whether the information needed for learning can be retained in a small representation of the training sample. This paper extends the connection between compression and learnability beyond binary classification. It first considers multiclass categorization, where predictions may belong to more than two categories.

For multiclass problems, the authors prove that learnability is equivalent to compression whose size grows logarithmically with sample size. They also show that uniform convergence implies constant-size compression. Using the compression–learnability connection, they establish equivalence between PAC and agnostic PAC learnability in this setting and derive a compactness theorem for learnability.

The picture changes for supervised learning with general loss functions. Maintaining the connection to learnability requires an approximate form of compression. Using this formulation, the authors show that PAC and agnostic PAC learnability can differ even when the loss takes only three values. The results identify both the reach of compression as a characterization of learning and a precise boundary to extending conclusions from classification.
neurips-2016-supervised-learning-through.tldr: Compression characterizes multiclass learnability, but extending the connection to general losses requires approximate compression and changes which learning notions are equivalent.

paragraphs: Estimating depth and surface orientation from one image requires predictions that agree geometrically across a scene. SURGE improves this consistency by reasoning about the planar surfaces depicted in the image. It adjusts predicted depths and surface normals toward inferred planes while preserving fine detail within objects.

The method first uses a four-stream convolutional network to predict depth, surface normals, planar-region likelihoods, and planar-boundary likelihoods at each pixel. A dense conditional random field then combines these outputs. Its constraints encourage depth and normal estimates to agree with one another and with the plane and boundary information. The formulation also allows gradients to pass back to the depth and normal networks.

The paper introduces plane-wise evaluation metrics intended to capture geometric consistency relevant to subsequent 3D editing applications. On NYU v2, the regularization yields a reported 30% relative improvement in planar consistency. This result concerns the coherence of reconstructed planar surfaces, showing how jointly reasoning about multiple predictions can improve the geometry inferred from a single image.
neurips-2016-surge-surface-regularized-g.tldr: SURGE jointly regularizes depth and surface normals using inferred planes, reporting a 30% relative improvement in planar consistency on NYU v2.

paragraphs: One way to investigate a neural network is to synthesize an input that strongly activates a particular neuron. This technique, activation maximization, aims to reveal what the neuron has learned to detect. The paper improves the interpretability and visual quality of these synthesized inputs by using a deep generator network as a learned prior.

The generator supplies learned image structure to the synthesis process, helping produce recognizable images that still activate the chosen neuron strongly. The authors report a substantial qualitative improvement over earlier activation-maximization results, with synthetic images that appear almost real. The resulting visualizations make learned features easier to interpret.

The prior also transfers well to new datasets and somewhat well to different network architectures without being retrained. That qualified transfer result suggests the learned image prior can be reused across multiple analysis settings. Beyond visualizing neurons, the method can serve as an image generator, producing novel and recognizable images. Its contribution therefore links network interpretation with visually coherent image synthesis.
neurips-2016-synthesizing-the-preferred-.tldr: A deep generator prior makes activation-maximizing images more realistic and interpretable, helping reveal the features individual neurons respond to.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much computation is fundamentally required to minimize an average of m convex functions. It studies access to the component functions through gradient and proximal oracles. By proving matching upper and lower complexity bounds, it identifies both achievable performance and limits on improvement within the analyzed access models.

The results show a significant difference between deterministic and randomized optimization. For smooth functions, accelerated gradient descent is optimal in the deterministic setting, while an accelerated version of SVRG is optimal in the randomized setting. Gradient access alone suffices to achieve the optimal rate for these smooth problems.

For nonsmooth functions, the available operation changes the answer: access to proximal oracles reduces complexity compared with gradient access alone. The authors develop optimal methods based on smoothing that exploit this advantage. Together, the results explain how smoothness, randomization, and oracle choice shape optimization difficulty, giving a principled basis for comparing methods that have different kinds of access to the objective.
neurips-2016-tight-complexity-bounds-for.tldr: Tight complexity bounds show how randomization and proximal access change the optimal cost of minimizing averages of convex functions.

paragraphs: A compact representation of a probability distribution is useful partly because of the operations it makes efficient. This paper studies that question for Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagrams, or PSDDs, a type of arithmetic circuit representation. Its focus is on combining distributions by multiplication and eliminating variables by summing them out.

The authors show that PSDDs support polynomial-time multiplication but do not support a polynomial-time operator for summing out variables. This establishes a specific combination of capabilities and limits. General arithmetic circuits do not support multiplication efficiently in all cases, so the PSDD result enables a broader class of applications involving that operation.

As a concrete use, the paper gives a compilation algorithm for probabilistic graphical models. Each factor of the model is first represented as a PSDD, and the factors are then multiplied together. The authors describe this procedure as simple and effective. The broader lesson is that efficient multiplication can make a representation useful for constructing probabilistic models even when other transformations remain intractable.
neurips-2016-tractable-operations-for-ar.tldr: PSDDs support efficient multiplication, enabling straightforward graphical-model compilation, but do not support a general polynomial-time summing-out operator.

paragraphs: Finding the best option in a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem requires learning from uncertain observations. When additional structure is known, checking that a proposed option is best can be easier than discovering that option initially. This paper builds a general framework around that difference between discovery and verification.

The analysis focuses on demands for very high confidence, expressed through a very small allowed failure probability δ. In this regime, the authors essentially show that identifying the best arm becomes as easy as verifying a candidate’s optimality. The result connects the cost of a full search with the potentially simpler task enabled by known problem structure.

The framework is applied to linear bandits, dueling bandits under the Condorcet assumption, Copeland dueling bandits, unimodal bandits, and graphical bandits. These applications improve the stated state of the art for the respective problems. The contribution is a reusable route to high-confidence identification guarantees across several structured settings, rather than a separate discovery strategy tailored to each one.
neurips-2016-verification-based-solution.tldr: A verification-based framework shows that high-confidence best-arm identification can essentially match verification difficulty in several structured bandit problems.
